newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland hails security pact, but says too general.
newsitem.headline: Poland hails security pact, but says too general.

text.p: Poland welcomed Tuesday's pact between NATO and Russia as a move to end an era of confrontation in Europe but the foreign minister said the treaty was imprecise and partnership with Moscow could be difficult.

"We welcome the signing of the Founding Act... It opens the way for a true partnership in Europe and ending a period of confrontation, which was characteristic for the Cold War," the foreign ministry said in a statement.

But Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said in a newspaper article that some of the agreement's provisions were too general and that Russia's good will in interpreting them would be needed to achieve a real partnership between Moscow and the Western military alliance.

"As most of such documents, it (the agreement) includes many clauses that are sometimes too general and phrases at times imprecise and subject to differing interpretations," Rosati wrote in Tuesday's Gazeta Wyborcza daily.

"The final nature of NATO-Russia relations will depend on many factors, including...Russia's will to implement provisions of the Act in good faith and in line with the vision of European security shared by most nations of our continent," he wrote.

Rosati said the NATO-Russia partnership envisaged by the treaty, signed in Paris by President Boris Yeltsin and heads of NATO countries, was likely to be difficult because many Russian politicians would continue to oppose the pact's eastward expansion.

"It (the NATO-Russia partnership) will probably not be easy. It would be naive to expect that the signing of the Act would instantly change the attitudes of the Russian elites and the way they view NATO and the process of its development," he wrote.

Rosati earlier said that Poland, hoping to be invited to join NATO at its July summit in Madrid, should have a place in a joint council between NATO and Russia, whose creation is one of the most important provisions of the Paris treaty.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- the former Soviet bloc's leaders in economic and democratic reforms -- are widely expected to be in the first batch of NATO entrants, which may join in 1999.
Some Polish politicians fear that because the council will be confined to NATO and Russia, Moscow would be closer to the pact than countries negotiating to join it and could slow the process.

Foreign ministry spokesman Boguslaw Majewski said Poland, which under the treaty cannot be part of the NATO-Russia council, would strive to be present during the accession negotiations period in as many NATO bodies as possible.

"The formula of the Russia-NATO council does not envisage the presence of other states. We think that our interests should be consulted in as many bodies as possible during the transition period," Majewski told Reuters.
